nodes.label: Creator
nodes.summary: Starts a resumable upload (POST returns a session URI, then PUT bytes) and can resume after a drop with Content-Range: bytes */N and a 308 response.
nodes.details: Limits: 256 GB or 12 hours, whichever is less (15 minutes by default for unverified accounts).

nodes.label: Upload / metadata API
nodes.summary: Creates the video record and the upload session. Keeps heavy bytes off application servers.

nodes.label: Raw upload store
nodes.summary: Object storage holding the original file. Kept so videos can be re-encoded with future codecs.

nodes.label: Job queue
nodes.summary: An object-created event triggers transcoding. Eventual consistency is fine: a new video may take minutes to become watchable.

nodes.label: Transcoding orchestrator (DAG)
nodes.summary: Splits the source into chunks, schedules encodes per chunk × rendition, then packaging, thumbnails and moderation. Tasks are idempotent and retryable per chunk.
nodes.details: Chunk length and ladder rungs in the baseline are illustrative. YouTube has not published them.

nodes.label: Transcoding workers + VCU chips
nodes.summary: YouTube built a custom Video (trans)Coding Unit and the software to coordinate it, reporting up to 20–33× compute-efficiency improvement over its previous optimised system. The next chip adds AV1.
nodes.details: Blog dated 2021-04-21. Whether every YouTube encode runs on the VCU is not stated.

nodes.label: Segments + manifests
nodes.summary: Immutable segments and HLS/DASH manifests in object storage. A master playlist lists renditions (EXT-X-STREAM-INF).
nodes.details: Segments are static, cacheable files, ideal for CDNs.

nodes.label: CDN / ISP caches
nodes.summary: Serves most playback bytes from the edge. Request coalescing stops a cache-miss stampede on viral uploads.
nodes.details: Google and Netflix both run ISP-embedded caches (Google Global Cache, Open Connect).

nodes.label: Metadata DB (Vitess / MySQL)
nodes.summary: Sharded relational store for videos and channels. Vitess was created at YouTube in 2010 to solve MySQL scalability, moving shard routing out of application code.

nodes.label: Search index
nodes.summary: Inverted index fed from metadata by change-data-capture. A new video may take seconds to appear.

nodes.label: Viewer
nodes.summary: Fetches the manifest, starts on a low rendition and adapts per segment from measured throughput and buffer.

nodes.label: View-event stream
nodes.summary: View events go to a stream and are aggregated in windows rather than UPDATE views = views+1, with fraud filtering in the stream.

steps.caption: The creator starts a resumable session. The API returns a session URI.
The file bytes are PUT to storage. After a dropped connection, an empty PUT with Content-Range: bytes */N returns 308 and the offset to resume from.
The finished upload triggers a transcoding job.
The orchestrator splits the video into chunks and plans encodes per chunk and rendition.
Workers encode in parallel, so wall-clock time follows the slowest chunk, not the video length. YouTube reports custom VCU chips doing this work.
Encoded segments and manifests are written as immutable files.
When the pipeline completes, the video is marked READY.
Change-data-capture updates the search index shortly after.
The player asks for the video's metadata and manifest URL.
Metadata comes from the sharded relational store.
The player fetches segments from the CDN, starting on a low rendition and adapting up or down per segment.
Only cache misses reach origin storage. Segments are immutable, so they cache well.
View events are streamed and aggregated in windows instead of updating a counter on every view.
The orchestrator schedules encodes per chunk and rendition.
A worker fails on one chunk. Tasks are idempotent, so only that chunk is retried, not the whole video.
The retried chunk writes its segment.
The video is marked READY only when the whole pipeline completes.
